### The problem TSS solves

**NORA:** Let's talk about the customer's problem. Explain the world TSS works in.

**JAMES:** Start with the regulation, as general background. If you make medicines, biologics or certain medical products in the US, you must follow what are called current good manufacturing practices, usually shortened to GMP, enforced by the Food and Drug Administration. GMP is broad, but a core idea is that you must be able to prove your processes and environment are under control. That means documented evidence.

**NORA:** And the environment includes the cleanrooms.

**JAMES:** Exactly. Cleanrooms are classified by how many particles of a given size are allowed per volume of air, under international standards. To keep a cleanroom in its class, you need filters that work, airflow that's right, pressure differences between rooms that keep contamination flowing the right way, and regular testing to prove it. Then there are biosafety cabinets, the enclosed workstations scientists use to handle infectious or sensitive material. Those need to be certified, typically on a regular schedule and after they're moved or repaired. And fume hoods, which protect people from chemical fumes.

**NORA:** And TSS does all of that?

**JAMES:** That's the core. Testing and certifying cleanrooms, biosafety cabinets, fume hoods and related equipment. Plus calibration, which means checking that instruments like thermometers, pressure gauges and balances read accurately against a known standard. Plus, through recent acquisitions, medical gas systems in hospitals, scientific refrigeration for things like vaccines and samples, and gas safety monitoring.

**NORA:** Why do customers outsource this?

**JAMES:** A few reasons, partly our inference. It's specialised and requires trained, certified technicians and calibrated test equipment. It's periodic, so a single site may not need a full-time person. And there's value in independence. An outside certifier is a credible third party when the auditor asks.

**NORA:** You said "recurring" earlier.

**JAMES:** Yes, and that's the heart of the business model. The private equity firm described the work as recurring on-site compliance at fixed intervals. A biosafety cabinet gets certified on a schedule. A cleanroom gets tested on a schedule. Calibration happens on a schedule. So once you have a customer, you tend to keep coming back. That's a lovely revenue profile for a services business.

**NORA:** Who inside the customer actually buys this?

**JAMES:** Usually a few people, in general terms. The quality assurance team, who care most about the documentation and audit-readiness. The facilities or engineering team, who care about the equipment working and about scheduling visits without disrupting production. The lab managers and scientists, who just want their cabinets and freezers to work. And in hospitals, the facilities and safety staff responsible for the medical gas systems. Procurement gets involved when contracts are renewed.

**NORA:** And they all want something slightly different.

**JAMES:** Right. Quality wants perfect paperwork. Facilities wants minimal disruption. Scientists want uptime. Procurement wants a lower price. A good vendor serves all four, and the one that makes the quality team's life easiest usually wins the renewal.

**NORA:** And the stakes for the customer?

**JAMES:** High. If an FDA inspection finds that a cleanroom's records are incomplete, or an instrument was out of calibration, it can mean findings that require corrective action, delays to product release and, in serious cases, much worse. TSS's own GMP page says its goal is that clients are always prepared for the next audit. That line sums up what customers are buying.

### Inside the service

**NORA:** Let's go a bit deeper. What does a TSS technician actually do on a visit?

**JAMES:** As a general picture, a technician arrives on site with calibrated test instruments. For a cleanroom, they might measure airflow velocity across the filters, test the filters for leaks, count particles at defined locations, check pressure differences between rooms and measure things like temperature and humidity. For a biosafety cabinet, they test airflow patterns, filter integrity and alarms. Each test has acceptance criteria. Pass or fail, the readings get recorded.

**NORA:** And then?

**JAMES:** Then the readings become a report or certificate. Which instrument was used, its calibration status, what was tested, the results, whether they met the standard, who did the work, when, and who reviewed it. In a GMP environment, that document is the evidence. If it's incomplete or inconsistent, it's a problem.

**NORA:** What about the newer businesses, medical gas and refrigeration? What do those technicians do?

**JAMES:** Medical gas, as general background, means the piped systems in hospitals and clinics that deliver oxygen, medical air, nitrous oxide and vacuum to patient rooms and operating theatres. Those systems are governed by fire and safety codes and have to be tested and certified, including after installation or repair. Get it wrong and patients are at risk. So it's specialised, high-stakes work, and again, every test ends in documentation.

**NORA:** And refrigeration?

**JAMES:** Shon's Scientific services the refrigerators and freezers that hold vaccines, biological samples and reagents. If a minus eighty freezer fails overnight, years of research samples can be lost. So customers care about preventive maintenance and fast repairs. And MDC Systems does gas detection and life-safety monitoring, the alarms that warn if a dangerous gas leaks in a lab or a semiconductor plant.

**NORA:** So the common thread is controlled, safety-critical environments.

**JAMES:** That's exactly it. Different equipment, same customer worry: prove it's safe and keep it working.

**NORA:** And how does TSS capture the data?

**JAMES:** It has proprietary software called eData, a field-data application that TSS says is compliant with an FDA regulation known as 21 CFR Part 11.

**NORA:** Explain Part 11.

**JAMES:** It's the part of the federal regulations that sets out when electronic records and electronic signatures can be trusted as equivalent to paper. Broadly, as general background, it requires things like audit trails, controls on who can change data, and secure electronic signatures. For a GMP customer, a vendor whose field software meets those requirements is a big deal, because otherwise the digital records might not be acceptable to an auditor.

**NORA:** And then customers see the records how?

**JAMES:** Through a portal called TSSConnect. From what TSS describes, customers can access, view and download their certificates and reports online. So when the auditor asks for the biosafety cabinet certification from March, the quality manager can pull it up.

**NORA:** And the quality system?

**JAMES:** TSS says its quality system is ISO 9001 certified. That's the international standard for quality management systems. So there's regulated-operations discipline in place: a quality system, compliant field software and a customer portal.

**NORA:** That's a stronger digital base than I expected.

**JAMES:** Me too, honestly. Many field services companies still run on paper forms and spreadsheets. TSS has structured digital capture of field data, which, in my view, is exactly the foundation AI needs. The data is already there, in a regulated format, from every visit.

**NORA:** But there's a catch with all those acquisitions.

**JAMES:** There usually is. The question is whether airandvac, Shon's, MDC and Heninger are on eData and TSSConnect yet, or still on their own systems. The acquisition releases emphasise that customers will see no service disruption, and that the acquired businesses keep their people and customer contacts. That's sensible for customers. But in our inference it also suggests those units are still running their own ways of working, at least for now.

### The people in the gowns

**NORA:** Before we get to AI, let's talk about the technicians, because everything depends on them.

**JAMES:** Agreed. A TSS technician needs technical training, knowledge of standards, the discipline to follow procedures exactly, and the ability to work in a gown in a cleanroom for hours. They also need to be good with customers, because they're often the only TSS person the customer sees. That's a rare combination.

**NORA:** And how does a technician feel about the paperwork?

**JAMES:** We have no TSS-specific evidence on that, so this is general. In most field services businesses, technicians would rather be fixing and testing than typing. Reports done at the end of a long day, or in the evening, are a common source of frustration and of errors. So a tool that cuts that work is likely to be welcomed, if it's genuinely easier.

**NORA:** And if it isn't?

**JAMES:** Then it's ignored, or worse, worked around. That's why I'd involve technicians in designing any AI tool. They know where the friction is: the fields that are always the same, the readings that have to be typed twice, the bits of the procedure that the form doesn't fit.

**NORA:** What about the acquired companies' technicians?

**JAMES:** They're a special case. They joined TSS through a deal they didn't choose. They're used to their own forms and their own way of working. Asking them to switch to eData is a change. If the switch comes with something that makes their day better, like faster reports, it's a much easier conversation. If it just feels like head office imposing a new system, you risk losing people, and in a technician-bound business, losing people is losing revenue.

**NORA:** And the quality reviewers?

**JAMES:** They're the other key group. They carry a lot of responsibility, because their sign-off is what makes the document trustworthy. AI that pre-checks reports helps them, but they'll want to understand exactly what it checks and what it doesn't. Trust in the tool has to be earned, report by report.

### The market and competitors

**NORA:** How big is the market?

**JAMES:** I'm going to be very direct. We didn't find a reliable market size figure for calibration, testing or cleanroom certification services in our sources. So I'm not going to give one.

**NORA:** What can we say about it?

**JAMES:** The segments, at least. Pharma, biotech, healthcare and life sciences are the core. Then the adjacent markets TSS has moved into: medical gas systems through airandvac and MDC, refrigeration for healthcare and biopharma through Shon's, and gas safety in semiconductor plants through MDC.

**NORA:** Semiconductors is a stretch from pharma.

**JAMES:** It's an interesting step. MDC's customers are primarily semiconductor and life sciences companies. Semiconductor fabrication also uses cleanrooms and hazardous gases, so the skills overlap. It widens the market TSS can serve, and in my view it's a hedge against relying on one industry.

**NORA:** And the demand drivers?

**JAMES:** Audit readiness, first. Outsourcing of recurring compliance work, second, which is our inference. And demand for single-vendor coverage across many asset types and sites, which is the logic of the roll-up. A big pharma company with ten sites would often rather have one vendor for cleanrooms, cabinets, calibration, refrigeration and gases than six different local firms.

**NORA:** Competitors?

**JAMES:** Our research was thin here, and I'll be honest about that. Two names came up. Quad City Testing Laboratory, which a CB Insights listing compares directly to TSS, though we didn't verify its offering or ownership. And Rogue Calibration, a calibration lab in La Jolla marketed for ISO and FDA compliance, which looks like a local rival. From general knowledge, Transcat is a publicly listed company that provides calibration services and is a well-known name in that space. And beyond that, the market is full of regional specialists, many of whom are exactly the kind of firms TSS acquires.

**NORA:** How does a national calibration company differ from TSS?

**JAMES:** In general terms, a calibration specialist like Transcat focuses on instruments, often with lab-based calibration where equipment is shipped in, as well as on-site work. TSS is broader on the physical environment side: rooms, cabinets, hoods, gas systems and refrigeration, mostly on site. They overlap in calibration, and both sell to life sciences. But TSS's pitch is coverage of the whole controlled environment, not just the instruments in it. That's our reading of the two models.

**NORA:** So the competitors are partly future acquisitions.

**JAMES:** That's often how roll-ups see the world. Today's local rival is tomorrow's add-on.

**NORA:** Could customers just do this themselves?

**JAMES:** Some could, especially for calibration. A large pharma company can buy its own calibration equipment and software and hire technicians. That's a threat we'd flag as an inference. But for cleanroom certification and biosafety cabinets, independence and specialised equipment make outsourcing attractive. And for smaller biotechs, building that capability in-house rarely makes sense.

**NORA:** Any AI-native challengers?

**JAMES:** None found in our sources. That doesn't mean there aren't any. But we didn't see a startup trying to automate cleanroom certification the way we've seen in, say, legal or environmental compliance. The physical testing still needs a person with instruments. The documentation is where the change would come.

### AI at TSS today

**NORA:** So, AI at TSS. Where are they?

**JAMES:** Honestly, no public evidence of AI at all. We looked at the website, the leadership page, the news releases and the TSSConnect page. No AI, no automation claims, no analytics claims. TSSConnect is described as access, viewing and download. eData is described as proprietary software, with no AI claim. There was one search result about advanced analytics and safety outcomes that we couldn't confirm was about TSS, so we've excluded it.

**NORA:** But the foundations are there.

**JAMES:** That's the key point. TSS has a chief information officer. It has a product development leader. It has structured field data in a Part 11-compliant system. It has an ISO 9001 quality system. It has a customer portal. Those are the building blocks. What it doesn't have, publicly, is any AI on top.

**NORA:** Is that a problem?

**JAMES:** Not yet, in my view. This isn't a market where customers are demanding AI from their certification vendor. But it's an opportunity, because the economics of the business are labour-heavy, and some of that labour is writing and reviewing documents that AI could help with.

**NORA:** Where else could AI show up for customers, beyond the reports?

**JAMES:** The portal is the obvious channel. Today TSSConnect lets customers view and download documents. Imagine instead a quality manager asking it, in plain English, "show me every biosafety cabinet across our three sites that failed a test in the last two years, and what was done." Or "which of our assets are due for certification before our inspection in June?" That's a search and summarisation job over records TSS already holds.

**NORA:** That sounds genuinely useful.

**JAMES:** It would be, and it's lower risk than drafting regulated records, because it's reading existing documents rather than creating new ones. The customer still sees the source certificates. I'd still validate it carefully, because a wrong answer before an inspection is a real problem. But it's a natural second step after report drafting.

**NORA:** And internally?

**JAMES:** Technician support. A new technician facing an unfamiliar cabinet model could ask an assistant for the procedure, the acceptance criteria and common failure causes, drawn from TSS's own procedures and past reports. That speeds up onboarding, which matters when you're absorbing technicians from four acquisitions.

**NORA:** And the regulatory angle?

**JAMES:** That's important. Anything that touches GMP records has to be validated. You can't just plug a generative AI tool into a regulated document workflow and hope for the best. The tool's role, its controls, its audit trail and the human review all have to be defined and tested. That slows things down, but it's also a moat. A vendor that figures out how to use AI in a compliant way has something hard to copy.

### A certification visit, step by step

**NORA:** Let's make it concrete. Walk me through a visit. Invented, not real.

**JAMES:** Let's say there's a mid-sized biotech in San Diego, call it Harbourline Bio. It has two cleanroom suites, twenty-four biosafety cabinets, a bank of laboratory freezers and a set of instruments that need calibration. TSS has a recurring contract. This week is the semi-annual cleanroom testing and the annual cabinet certification.

**NORA:** Who shows up?

**JAMES:** Two technicians, call them Marco and Lin. They arrive at seven, sign in, gown up. They've got their test instruments, each with a current calibration certificate. Over two days, they test the cleanrooms: filter leak tests, airflow, particle counts at each location, room pressures. Then they work through the cabinets one by one.

**NORA:** And they record everything in eData.

**JAMES:** Yes, on tablets. Each reading goes into the app, tied to the asset, the location and the instrument used. When a reading fails, say one cabinet's airflow is out of range, they note it, maybe make an adjustment, retest and record both results.

**NORA:** Then what?

**JAMES:** Then the report. For each cabinet, a certificate. For the cleanrooms, a full test report with every reading, the acceptance criteria and a pass-fail summary. Then a quality reviewer at TSS checks the reports before they're issued. Are all fields complete? Do the instrument serial numbers match? Are the results consistent with the criteria? Are signatures in place?

**NORA:** How long does that take?

**JAMES:** We don't know TSS's actual numbers, and I won't invent them. But in general, for field services in regulated environments, documentation and review can be a significant share of total time. Technicians may finish reports in the evening or the next day. Reviewers may find errors and send them back. And customers wait for their certificates.

**NORA:** And the customer?

**JAMES:** Harbourline's quality manager, call her Ana, wants the certificates quickly, because until she has them, she may not be able to release equipment for use. And she wants a clear summary: what failed, what was fixed, what needs follow-up. If one freezer is drifting warm, she wants to know before it fails.

**NORA:** Now replay it with AI.

**JAMES:** Marco and Lin do exactly the same physical testing. That doesn't change. But when they finish each cabinet, the system drafts the certificate from the eData readings straight away. It checks completeness, flags anything inconsistent, like an instrument whose calibration expires next week, and writes a plain-language summary of any failures and corrective actions. The technician reviews and signs on the spot.

**NORA:** And the quality reviewer?

**JAMES:** Instead of checking every field by hand, the reviewer gets a pre-checked report with the AI's flags highlighted, and focuses on judgement: is this adjustment acceptable, does this failure need escalation? Then the reviewer signs. Ana gets her certificates the same day, with a summary page across all twenty-four cabinets and a note that one freezer is trending warm.

**NORA:** So the testing is human and the paperwork is assisted.

**JAMES:** Exactly. And crucially, every step has a human signature, an audit trail and validated logic. That's what makes it acceptable in a GMP world.

### The challenges

**NORA:** Let's talk challenges.

**JAMES:** I'd name five. First, integration. Nine dated acquisitions under the current owner, four in the last year, plus more than twenty before that under previous leadership. Each acquired business has its own customers, people, processes and possibly its own software. Our inference is that several are still running on their own systems. That makes any network-wide AI effort harder.

**NORA:** Second?

**JAMES:** Second, disclosure. Revenue, headcount and customer numbers aren't public. That's normal for a private company, but it means we can't measure the value of anything. Internally, the challenge is similar. To build a business case for AI report drafting, you need to know how many hours technicians and reviewers spend on documents per visit. If that isn't measured consistently across acquired units, you're guessing.

**NORA:** Third?

**JAMES:** Third, validation. In a GMP environment, software that touches records must be validated. Adding AI means defining exactly what it does, testing it and documenting it, and repeating that when the model or the logic changes. It's manageable, but it's real work.

**NORA:** Fourth?

**JAMES:** Fourth, talent. A model built on more than four hundred technicians depends on hiring and keeping skilled people. If technicians are scarce, that limits growth. AI can't replace the person holding the instrument, so it can only help by making their time more productive.

**NORA:** And fifth?

**JAMES:** Fifth, service quality during integration. Customers pay TSS for reliability and audit-readiness. If an integration disrupts scheduling or record quality, it erodes the very thing customers value. That's why the acquisition releases promise "no service disruption." Keeping that promise across many integrations at once is hard.

**NORA:** Is the move into semiconductors a challenge too?

**JAMES:** It could be, in my view. Semiconductor customers are a different culture from pharma. Different standards, different buying processes, sometimes much larger and more demanding facilities. MDC knows that world, but TSS as a whole is a life sciences company. Managing two different customer bases well, without diluting focus, takes deliberate effort. On the other hand, it's a big, growing industry with heavy investment in new fabrication plants in the US, as general background, so it's an attractive adjacency.

**NORA:** Let me push on that first one. Is integration really necessary? If each acquired business is working fine, why disrupt it?

**JAMES:** Fair challenge. You don't have to integrate everything. But some things are worth integrating: one field data system, one customer portal, one scheduling view. Otherwise, a customer with sites in California and Massachusetts gets two different experiences from the same company, and you can't cross-sell or use AI across the network. My view is integrate the data and the customer experience, and leave local relationships and know-how alone.

### Opportunities

**NORA:** Opportunities.

**JAMES:** The first and biggest is AI-drafted service reports and GMP certificates from eData field data, with human sign-off. The payoff is in technician and quality review hours, across a network of more than four hundred technicians. That's our inference on the size of the prize, since we don't have hours per visit.

**NORA:** Second?

**JAMES:** Technician scheduling and route optimisation, especially across the newer sites in Utah, Arizona, Massachusetts and San Jose. Planning who goes where, with which instruments, to which customers, while respecting each customer's audit calendar. The payoff is less travel time and better margin.

**NORA:** Third?

**JAMES:** Consolidating every acquired brand's records into TSSConnect. One portal for every customer. The payoff is retention and cross-selling. If a customer sees all their certificates in one place, they're more likely to give TSS more of their sites and assets.

**NORA:** Fourth?

**JAMES:** Cross-selling across the family. Medical gas from airandvac and MDC, and refrigeration from Shon's, sold into existing cleanroom and lab customers. A biotech that already uses TSS for cabinets might also need its freezers serviced and its gas systems monitored.

**NORA:** And pricing?

**JAMES:** Recurring contracts tied to audit calendars. If TSS can show that it keeps a customer audit-ready across all asset types, it can price on that value rather than per visit. Our inference. And further add-ons in under-served regions like the Mountain West and Midwest. The owner said in 2022 it planned more acquisitions, and it has followed through.

**NORA:** And is there a data product hiding in here?

**JAMES:** Possibly, and I'd label it speculative. TSS sees test results across many cabinets, freezers and cleanrooms over time. Patterns in that data might predict which equipment is likely to fail or drift. A predictive maintenance alert, sent through TSSConnect, could become a premium service. But you'd need clean, consistent data across the network first, and clear agreements with customers about how their data is used.

**NORA:** Let's do a second walk-through. Scheduling across the new sites. Invented.

**JAMES:** Picture the new Utah operation from the Heninger deal. A scheduler, call him Dave, plans visits for a dozen technicians across Utah and neighbouring states. Each customer has a calendar of due dates: cabinets due in March, a cleanroom due in April, a freezer service every quarter. Some customers can only allow access on certain days. Some technicians are certified for medical gas, some aren't.

**NORA:** And today he does it how?

**JAMES:** Probably in a mix of spreadsheets, a scheduling tool and phone calls, which is common in businesses like this. When a technician is sick or a customer reschedules, Dave rebuilds the week by hand. Technicians sometimes drive two hours to a site for one cabinet because the schedule didn't group visits well.

**NORA:** And with an AI scheduling assistant?

**JAMES:** The system looks at every due date, access window, technician skill and location, and proposes a week that minimises driving while keeping every customer inside their compliance window. When something changes, it proposes a revised plan in seconds and Dave approves it. And because it sees all the family companies, it can spot that a hospital getting its medical gas certified next week also has two cabinets due next month, and suggest combining the visits.

**NORA:** That's cross-selling through scheduling.

**JAMES:** Exactly. And it only works if the acquired businesses' customer and asset data sit in one place. Which brings us back, again, to integration.

**NORA:** And what does all this mean for the customer, in the end?

**JAMES:** Fewer surprises. Certificates that arrive faster and are right the first time. A single view of every asset across every site. Early warning when equipment is drifting. And visits planned around their production schedule rather than the vendor's convenience. For a quality manager like our invented Ana, that's the difference between dreading the next audit and being ready for it.

**NORA:** It's interesting that none of that is flashy AI.

**JAMES:** It isn't, and I think that's the point. The most valuable AI in field services is often invisible to the customer. They just notice that things got faster and more reliable.

### The best AI bet and the first hundred days

**NORA:** If you had to pick one AI bet for the next eighteen months?

**JAMES:** AI-drafted field reports and certificates from eData, with human quality sign-off. It reuses data TSS already captures, it sits in the core recurring workflow, it touches every visit and it doesn't change the physical work customers rely on.

**NORA:** How would you run the first hundred days?

**JAMES:** Days one to thirty: measure first. How long do technicians spend on documentation per visit? How long does quality review take? How many reports are sent back for corrections, and why? How long until a customer receives a certificate? Do this in two or three established locations already on eData. Then write the validation plan with the quality team, because in GMP, validation isn't an afterthought.

**NORA:** Days thirty to sixty?

**JAMES:** Build and validate a narrow version. One report type, say biosafety cabinet certificates, which are high-volume and fairly standard. The AI drafts the certificate and the summary from eData readings, runs completeness and consistency checks, and flags issues. Technicians and reviewers use it alongside the existing process, and every output is compared.

**NORA:** And sixty to a hundred?

**JAMES:** Measure the difference: documentation time, review time, error rates, time to certificate. Ask customers like our invented Ana whether the summaries help. If the results are good, extend to cleanroom reports, then plan to bring the acquired units onto eData so they can benefit too. That last step makes AI a reason to integrate, not just a cost of integration.

**NORA:** What does validation actually involve? It sounds abstract.

**JAMES:** In general terms, for computerised systems in GMP settings, you write down what the system is supposed to do, its intended use, then you test that it does exactly that, document the tests, control changes and keep it under review. For AI drafting, you'd define the narrow job: take these eData fields, produce this certificate format, flag these specific inconsistencies. Then you test it against many real past reports and prove the outputs match. A free-form chatbot writing whatever it likes would be very hard to validate. A narrow, structured drafting tool is much more manageable.

**NORA:** And governance?

**JAMES:** A short, clear policy: the AI drafts, a qualified human signs, every AI action is logged in the audit trail, the logic is validated, and customer data isn't used to train external models. Share that policy with customers' quality teams. They'll appreciate being asked rather than surprised.

**NORA:** Who owns it?

**JAMES:** The chief information officer, partnered with the head of quality and operations, but with one named owner accountable for the result. And I'd make sure technicians help design it, because they'll be the ones using it on the floor of a cleanroom in a gown and gloves.

### Lessons for other businesses

**NORA:** What can other businesses learn from TSS?

**JAMES:** Four lessons. First, if every job ends in a document, your AI opportunity is the document. Many field services businesses, whether it's elevators, fire systems, lab equipment or HVAC, produce a report after every visit. That's structured data plus repetitive writing, which is where AI helps most.

**NORA:** Second?

**JAMES:** Second, digitise the field data before you think about AI. TSS's eData system is the hidden asset here. A company still on paper forms has to fix that first.

**NORA:** Third?

**JAMES:** Third, in regulated industries, compliance is the moat, not the obstacle. Validation and audit trails slow you down, but they also slow down competitors. The firm that does AI in a validated, auditable way first has something durable.

**NORA:** Fourth?

**JAMES:** Fourth, use AI as a reason to integrate. Acquired units often resist moving to central systems. If moving to the central system brings faster reports and less evening paperwork, the move sells itself.

**NORA:** Any lesson about acquisitions in particular?

**JAMES:** Yes. Promising "no disruption" to customers is the right message at the time of a deal. But it can become an excuse never to integrate. The best roll-ups, in my view, keep the promise to customers while steadily changing what happens behind the scenes: one data system, one portal, one way of scheduling. Customers should only notice that service got better.

**NORA:** I'd add a fifth: measure before you build.

**JAMES:** Absolutely. You can't prove AI saved hours if you never counted the hours.

### Risks and what to watch

**NORA:** Risks.

**JAMES:** One, AI-led testing and documentation entrants could reduce the value of manual report writing, which is a core part of what customers pay for. Two, customers insourcing calibration with their own instruments and software. Three, integration failure across many acquired brands eroding service quality. Four, technician shortages limiting growth. Most of those are our inferences, not reported events.

**NORA:** And pricing? If AI cuts the documentation time, what happens to what TSS charges?

**JAMES:** It depends on how TSS prices today, which we don't know. If it charges per asset certified, efficiency becomes margin. If it bills partly by technician time, efficiency could reduce revenue unless pricing shifts. In my view, a services company in this position should move toward pricing on outcomes, an audit-ready programme per site, so it keeps the benefit of its own efficiency.

**NORA:** Anything else on risk?

**JAMES:** One more, regulatory change. If the FDA or standards bodies change testing frequencies or requirements, demand could rise or fall. Stricter rules generally mean more work for TSS. Looser rules could mean less. That cuts both ways and we don't see a specific change coming in our sources. And there's concentration risk if a big share of revenue comes from a few large pharma customers, though we don't know TSS's customer mix.

**NORA:** And for the owners?

**JAMES:** Timing and story. About four and a half years in, with an accelerating acquisition pace. A buyer would want to see a well-integrated platform with consistent systems and margins, not a collection of local brands. AI report drafting, done well, is a visible proof of integration and operational maturity.

**NORA:** What should listeners watch?

**JAMES:** Four things. First, more add-ons, and whether they move further into semiconductors or stay in life sciences. Second, any announcement that acquired businesses have moved onto eData and TSSConnect. Third, any AI or automation claim on TSS's site, especially around reporting. And fourth, any new detail on revenue or scale.

### Wrap-up

**NORA:** Let me try a summary. Technical Safety Services is a La Jolla-based company, founded in 1970, that tests, calibrates and certifies cleanrooms, biosafety cabinets, fume hoods, medical gas systems, refrigeration and gas safety equipment for pharma, biotech, healthcare, life sciences and now semiconductor customers. It has more than four hundred technicians and a recurring, schedule-driven business. Levine Leichtman bought it in June 2022, and it has made at least nine dated add-ons since, four of them between November 2025 and July 2026. It has a compliant field-data system called eData, a customer portal called TSSConnect and an ISO 9001 quality system, but no visible AI. In our view, the best opportunity is AI-drafted reports and certificates from field data, validated and signed by humans, and using that to bring the acquired businesses onto one platform.

**JAMES:** And my closing thought. In regulated industries, the work isn't finished until the paperwork is right. That makes the paperwork the place where AI can do the most good, as long as a person still signs their name.
